messages.author: 9f2f94d52d251a63
messages.subject: high estimates in nulloccupancy model
parts:
Hey everyone,

I am running null models for two species using occu(). For the first one I am getting an occupancy estimate of 1, which makes sense because it occurs at least once at all sites. For the second species I am getting an occupancy estimate of 0.998. I am very confused by this because it only occurs at ~40% of the sites. It seems as though the model is underestimating detection probability (estimates at ~13%), but I don't know why. Any idea why this could be? Below is the detection history. Thanks in advance for any help!

- Jesse

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] high estimates in nulloccupancy model
parts:
Hi Jesse,

 

It could be that the species 2 is really underdetected so much (and the estimate of p of 0.13 seems to suggest so), but in addition, site-occupancy models are also known to produce biased estimates of psi and p when p is low, where “low” typically means something in the region of 0.2 or below. See the simulation results in the original occupancy paper 2002. If you have access to the book Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology (Kéry & Royle, 2016), we also say this and demonstrate it using a simulation in chapter 10.

 

Best regards  --Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] high estimates in nulloccupancy model
parts:
This is definitely an issue with maximum likelihood estimate for these problems:  when the true detection probability is low, there is a tendency for the maximum likelihood estimate to be 1.0 for psi.  As support that occu is doing everything correctly consider the log of the likelihood surface:


The red dot shows the maximum likelihood estimates for psi and p.

Going Bayesian is a step forward but it's not just about the posterior means:  the posterior variance and the shape of the posterior distribution needs to be taken into account.  Here are the marginal posterior distributions of psi and p when the prior is a uniform distribution:
​

So one can't rule out a value near 1.0 for psi even if one is a Bayesian.

Jim
​

Thanks for your help everybody
- Jesse

For 7 of the 8 sites where the species was detected, it was detected on only a single visit. You wouldn't get detection histories like that if detection probability were high.
